BACKGROUND
Electric propulsion is not a new concept. Electric commercial vessels carrying passengers started
becoming more common after the creation of electric propulsion in the 19th century, but were quickly
diminished around 1920, when gasoline outboard motors grew popular due to convenience and extended
running time [1].
Though production of electric vessels slowed, it was never halted. Electric vessels proved to be
essential for the military during the Cold War and their development led to crucial advancements in battery
and motor control technology that are still in use today [1]. Electric propulsion offers significant
advantages in environmental sustainability, noise reduction, efficiency, and operational flexibility that are
continuously growing the technology, especially in military applications [1]. Naval and marine
engineering provides the fundamental basis for developing the vessels and nautical technology that keeps
our country safe. Since the Navy’s creation over 250 years ago, engineers have been at the forefront of
innovation to support the ever-changing and developing needs of the military.
The East Carolina University PEP boat team entered the Uncrewed: Open division for the 2026
competition to further investigate the modernization of marine technologies in electric propulsion and
innovations in remote control ships. The objective of the team is to develop a fully remote-controlled
vessel that can complete a two-mile course with a 180° turn in less than 55 minutes and carry a 60-pound
payload. The vessel is also limited to a total voltage of less than or equal to 55.5V and a total power
capacity below 500 Ah. To accomplish the objectives, the team elected to fully fabricate a hull specific to
this application. Through research and verification, the optimal material, hull design, and hull shape to
produce a lightweight and fast but stable vessel were selected. Additionally, each propulsion component
was researched and selected with the goal of optimizing the speed and efficiency of the vessel.

When formulating the hull design, the team prioritized speed, stability, and maneuverability, while
also considering the vessel’s ability to house the required propulsion components. The design that fulfilled
all requirements was the catamaran style, specifically modeled from Mystic Powerboats’ Miss GEICO.
This style offers many advantages to the specific competition course having long straight runs with
minimal turns. The narrow twin hulls minimize the wetted surface, allowing for fast acceleration, while
the low-profile design reduces air resistance, and, therefore, drag. The bridge of the hull provides an open
gap in the hull that contributes to higher efficiency at top speeds.

PROPULSION
The twin-motor electric catamaran presented in this paper integrates a high-reliability control
system, high-RPM electric propulsion, water-cooled motor controllers, a multi-battery power system, and
a wire steering mechanism. The design emphasizes controllability, safety, and operational durability
within competition constraints and the possibility for future performance improvements.
The safety system centers around high-current battery disconnect switches and fuses. This system
provides independent on/off control for the propulsion and control battery banks, enabling immediate
shutdown of propulsion power while keeping the control system active for steering and remote sensing.
Redundant kill switches ensure propulsion can be disabled even if one system fails. The propulsion circuit
routes the 48V battery through the fuses and disconnect switches before reaching the electric speed
controllers (ESCs), while the control circuit routes the 12V battery through another disconnect switch and
universal battery eliminator circuit (UBEC) to the receiver, servo, and pump. This system meets
competition safety requirements and maintains steering capabilities during emergency propulsion
shutdown.
The system is organized into five major subsystems: The control system that provides throttle and
steering commands; The propulsion system converts electrical energy into thrust; The motor control
system regulates motor speed and protects against overload; The power system distributes high-current
and low-voltage energy to all integrated electronics; The steering and cooling systems maintain directional
power and thermal stability. These subsystems operate as an integrated whole, ensuring that the catamaran
can deliver consistent performance under varying load and environmental conditions. A high‑level
overview of subsystem interactions is shown in Figure 4.

The control system is built around a FLYSKY FSi6 transmitter paired with an FSiA6 receiver,
powered by a dedicated 12V 10 Ah LiFePO4 battery feeding a 5V UBEC. This subsystem provides
throttle, steering, and auxiliary pulse width modulation (PWM) control with low latency and stable
automatic frequency hopping digital system (AFHDS) 2A spread spectrum communication [16]. The
independent control battery prevents brownouts and ensures uninterrupted operation of the receiver, servo,
and cooling pump even during high current operation. The receiver interfaces directly with the ESCs for
throttle control and with the high torque steering servo for rudder actuation, while the UBEC supplies
regulated power to all low voltage electronics. Waterproof wiring, grommets, and sealed connectors ensure
reliable operation in a marine environment.
The vessel uses two 48.1V 22000mAh Li-Po to power our mirrored “dual-motored” propulsion
system. To maximize efficiency and minimize weight, the power consumption of the motors was
calculated to determine the capacity required from the batteries to complete the race.

This approach links battery sizing to propulsion requirements, ensuring the energy system is not
oversized or undersized for our application. To ensure our vessel would safely complete the race, a battery
slightly larger capacity than necessary was selected to account for heat dissipation and other inefficiencies
that may be faced in a real situation.
A dual-motor configuration was chosen to distribute load, reducing per-motor current draw and
thermal stress but still being able to support operation within optimal efficiency ranges. This configuration
improves reliability and avoids the performance limitations associated with a single motor operating near
its maximum capacity. The propulsion system utilizes two 20 kW brushless DC motors [17]. These motors
were selected to meet the required power demands, as they provide high RPM and torque relative to their
power rating and are compatible with the competition’s 55.5 V requirement. Each motor is capable of 14
kW continuous output with peak power near 20 kW [17]. This matches the discharge capability of the LiPo battery packs.
The motors operate within a 48–55.5V range and draw approximately 280A continuous, directly
aligning with the selected 48V battery system to minimize electrical losses and ensure efficient power
transfer [17]. Their ability to achieve 25,000 RPM under load [17] is critical for reaching high speeds.
Additionally, the motors are designed for marine environments, featuring liquid cooling jackets, and
corrosion resistant materials, ensuring reliability and consistent performance under operating conditions.
The two 48.1V batteries will be protected by 400A fuses and QS10 anti‑spark connectors.
Marine‑grade 6 AWG and 8 AWG wiring, terminal blocks, and lugs, provide corrosion‑resistant,
vibration‑tolerant electrical distribution. Electrical integration uses waterproof connectors, heat‑shrink

[18]. These controllers convert direct current (DC) battery power into three-phase alternating current

cooling loop to ensure continuous heat removal. The ESCs are connected via a control area network
(CAN) bus, with a master ESC controlling the second ESC to provide seamless, simultaneous, and equal
power output. This design sacrifices differential steering capability in favor of improved simplicity,
reliability, and operational safety. Their high current rating and proven reliability in marine applications
make them well-suited for the vessel’s power demands.

The propeller of the boat is responsible for delivering the power from the motor to push the boat
forward. The propeller must be able to deliver high top speed, maintain stability, and accelerate quickly
enough to get the boat on plane. A higher number of blades gives the propeller more surface area, causing
a higher drag force, but reducing the chance of cavitation. For this application, a three-blade propeller was
considered the best option, as it can produce high top speeds while also mitigating cavitation. The propeller
needs to be made of a material strong enough to withstand the forces of the moving water without flexing
or vibrating. The most common materials for propellers are aluminum and stainless steel.
Propeller pitch is defined as the theoretical distance the boat travels forward with each rotation of
the propeller. A high-pitch propeller can push the boat farther with one rotation, meaning it is more
efficient on the battery, reaches a higher top speed, but has lower acceleration. A lower-pitch propeller
reaches a lower top speed and is less efficient on the battery, but it provides higher acceleration and can
push the boat on plane faster. A propeller with a larger diameter requires more torque from the motor to
accelerate, but it produces more thrust than a smaller-diameter propeller, allowing the boat to travel faster.
For the applications of our vessel, a smaller propeller with a pitch-to-diameter ratio of 2.0 was chosen.
The greatest risk of damage to the propeller is cavitation, which occurs when the water pressure drops
below the vapor pressure, causing vapor bubbles that lead to accelerated erosion and pitting. The study in
Figure 11 examines the local water pressure around the propeller and compares it to the water vapor
pressure under the expected operation speed of the vessel, 40 miles per hour, showing that the propeller
will experience moderate cavitation. Cavitation does not typically cause immediate damage, so by
implementing an inspection process and replacing
propellers, when necessary, damage by cavitation can
be mitigated.

Once the desired finish was complete, wax mold release was applied
to the foam prior to fiberglass lamination. Then, fiberglass was applied
in three layers all around the mold using polyester resin. After curing
for two days, the fiberglass mold was removed from the foam.
Unfortunately, the mold release did not work as intended, even while
intently following the instructions. The team believes this is because a
layer of primer paint was not applied to the foam prior to the mold
release application. Fiberglass filler is a slightly porous material, so
without something to seal this off, the mold release was absorbed into
the Bondo rather than laying on top of it. Due to this, the foam was
difficult to remove from the fiberglass and some damage occurred in
the process. To remedy these areas, fiberglass patches were laminated
on the inside and outside of the mold to increase strength and smooth
out the finish. The patched mold is shown in Figure 15.
A wooden structure was constructed to support the mold from the
outside to preserve stability without compromising interior finish. At
this point, the mold was ready for mold release, but instead of using a
wax release, the team decided to use exterior sheathing tape. This tape
has a nonstick exterior and is made to be water and airtight so no leaks
of epoxy resin or air would escape.
Time is limited when working with epoxy resin after being mixed
with hardener, so the team had to be fully prepared before laminating
the carbon fiber. Structural members were made using the exact carbon
fiber, resin, and vacuum bagging techniques that were to be used on the
hull. This allowed the team to practice on less crucial components to get
an idea of what working with the material was like. It was found that
the resin would start to harden and become unworkable in about one
hour. Therefore, the team knew it would be a race to apply all four layers
of carbon fiber. To reduce the risk of hardener setting up during the
process, the team made templates of sections of the boat. This allowed
the carbon fiber to be cut and organized, which reduces the amount of
scrambling during the lay-up process. Additionally, all vacuum
bagging materials were cut to shape and laid out so they were ready to
apply. Figure 16 shows the team in the process of vacuum-bagging the
hull.

allowed the epoxy resin to harden while pressure was being applied.

exact position that allows the bow to be pushed down to prevent the vessel from capsizing. Fiberglass and

the forward section housing the disconnect switch leads; the midsection containing the fuses, propulsion

epoxied and fiber glassed into the hull structure. The motors

the forward section housing the disconnect switch leads; the midsection containing the fuses, propulsion

steering assembly, and cooling system. This compartmentalized layout improves weight distribution,
reduces wire and shaft routing complexity, and gives accessibility for inspection and maintenance. Each
propulsion motor is mounted to a custom carbon‑fiber‑reinforced, 3D‑printed motor mount that was
epoxied and fiber glassed into the hull structure. The motors
are secured to the mounts using their face‑plate mounting
screws and additional pipe clamps to prevent deflection or
rotation under high torque loads as shown in Figure 19.

diameter stainless‑steel propeller shaft, matching the motor
shaft diameter to ensure proper alignment and torque

FULL VESSEL TESTING
Testing was conducted at the North Recreational Complex in
Greenville, North Carolina, where the vessel (Figure 25) was
evaluated at varying speeds to assess maneuverability and turning
performance under both loaded and unloaded conditions. Results
indicated that the waterline was lower than expected and overall
performance was slower than anticipated, with a maximum
observed speed of approximately 11 mph. Although the vessel was
unable to plane during the current testing phase, the motors
generated sufficient thrust to propel the boat forward. Steering
performance was stable at higher speeds but required adjustment to
allow a wider operational angle range, as the vessel exhibited a
tendency to track to the right due to hull shape. The cooling system
and control systems performed as intended, with minimal water
seepage observed throughout testing (Figure 26). Controller
connectivity remained reliable at distances up to approximately 500
feet. Propeller sizing was identified as insufficient and will require
adjustment, and the acceleration curve may need refinement to
provide smoother throttle response. Testing conditions limited the
ability to attempt full-speed operation, indicating that further testing
is required under more suitable conditions and location.

RISK
Developing a competition ready vessel from scratch introduces a wide range of risks, many of
which stem from uncertainties in fabrication, electrical integration, and hydrodynamics. While not all risks
can be eliminated, they can be systematically identified, assessed, and mitigated to reduce their likelihood
and impact. Most risks are physical or mechanical in nature, where failures could cause the vessel to sink,
lose propulsion, or become unsafe to operate. Before the fabrication process began, the team identified
potential risks and worked to create a design that mitigated those risks.
1. The risk of capsizing was a major consideration during the design process. The catamaran style
hull prevents capsizing by providing stability through its wide base and allowing weight to be
evenly distributed.
2. The risk of bow stuffing in rough water was a key consideration that significantly influenced the
boat’s design. Originally, the team planned to design a six-foot-long vessel, but after further
research and consultation with experienced members in the field, the team increased the length to
eight feet to allow the weight to be placed further back. Thus, transferring the center of gravity
further back in the vessel, allowing the bow buoyancy to ride over the waves.
3. With any marine device, a concern is water leakage. Leaks forming during operation increase
weight, reduce stability, and may cause the vessel to sink. To mitigate this risk, positive buoyancy
foam is included to keep the vessel afloat even if fully flooded. Additional waterproofing measures
include sealed stuffing boxes, marine grade heat shrink, sealed connectors, internal coatings, and
an external gel coat.
4. Propeller failure is a concern that has very high impact if it were to happen. Failure would
immediately compromise vessel performance. Redundancy is provided through the twin motor
configuration, and propellers are fabricated with strength margins exceeding expected loads.

5. The risk of back drive was identified due to the potential for mechanical damage during improper
operation. Rapid transitions from high RPM to low RPM can cause torque to be driven back
through the propulsion system. To mitigate this risk, drivetrain couplings were selected to act as a
mechanical point of failure, protecting the motors. Additionally, the ESCs are programmed with
RPM transition limits to prevent rapid deceleration.
As previously mentioned, not all risks can be mitigated completely. The team thoughtfully worked
during the design and fabrication process to minimize the unavoidable risks during the competition.
These include:
1. As indicated earlier, the nature of the catamaran design allows for dual motors. This set up
introduces redundancy in the case one system fails.
2. Signal loss between the controller and the vessel is a low concern because the communication
system has a range exceeding the racecourse. In the case signal is lost, the team relies on failsafe
programming in the ESCs and propulsion components that removes power to the motor.
3. If emergency access to the inside of the hull is needed, rapid removal thumbscrews were used to
secure the top of the hull in place.
4. Motors and ESCs are expected to heat up during sustained use, which may cause thermal damage,
reduced efficiency, or inoperability. To mitigate this risk, water cooling jackets circulate cold water
around the motors and ESCs to maintain safe operating temperatures and preserve performance.
5. The risk of electronic failure was a critical concern due to the vessel’s reliance on electrical systems
for propulsion. Wiring issues or battery abnormalities could result in a total loss of propulsion. All
electrical systems were extensively tested after wiring and integration. ESCs are programmed with
internal protections, and fuses and manual kill switches provide safe system shutdown in the event
of failure.
6. The risk of battery fire, while unlikely, is treated as a high‑severity condition. Mitigation relies on
conservative electrical limits, fuse protection, secure wiring practices, and pre‑ and post‑run
inspections to pinpoint potential issues early.
